rv.q: Together, they create a world that feels like the inside of an old jukebox: full of half-remembered stories, crackling melancholy, and music that never quite stops playing.
Cavils aside, this remains a very special piece of theatre and I would urge anyone to catch McPherson’s own production of his work before it disappears for ever.
In those moments, quibbles fall away, leaving just the forlorn beauty of it all.
Here, at a late preview, I was impressed yet oddly unmoved.
The use of Dylan's compositions, raised to a level of harmonics and orchestration which far outstrips the original material is a coup in itself
There’s a slow and stoic beauty to the staging that makes it strangely engaging as it meanders through its own bleakness.
The music is the evening's self-evident glory: a refresher course in the extraordinary output of the 2016.
It's a beautiful, technically accomplished production that keeps you at arm's length when it should be drawing you close.
Feel-good it ain’t, but there’s no denying that Girl from the North Country is a skilfully executed, poignant and powerful piece.
To this reviewer, it felt like it was still in need of tightening up, so it didn’t manage to quite blow me away.
But I can’t help feeling like I’m missing something.

cn.t: McPherson's Depression-era Dylan jukebox musical returns to the Old Vic to mostly warm reviews. Critics praise its atmospheric staging and reimagined songs, though some find the relentless gloom wears thin.
